title: Fraud Detection and Forensics
answer: Expense fraud, money laundering networks, vendor fraud, communication forensics and tracing digital assets.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Expense Fraud
children.blurb: Expense fraud is the deliberate submission of false, inflated, or duplicate expense claims for reimbursement, whether by an employee, a manager, or an outside party working with an insider.

children.name: Money Laundering Networks
children.blurb: Money laundering networks are the connected sets of people, accounts, companies, and payment channels used to move and disguise the origin of criminal proceeds.

children.name: Phantom Vendors and Procurement Fraud
children.blurb: Phantom vendors and procurement fraud covers fake suppliers, shell companies, and real suppliers billing for goods or services that were never delivered.

children.name: Communication Forensics
children.blurb: Communication forensics is the examination of messages, call records, and collaboration data to reconstruct what happened, who knew what, and when.

children.name: Tracing and Recovering Digital Assets
children.blurb: Tracing and recovering digital assets covers the work of following value across blockchains and related systems after fraud, theft, ransomware, or insolvency, then trying to return it to victims or creditors.

sections.body: Fraud detection and forensics is the work of finding financial deception, proving what happened, and following value as it moves. In practice, artificial intelligence is used to score expense claims, flag unusual payment patterns, cluster accounts that behave alike, and read large volumes of messages for signs of coordination. Banks and payment firms run models that compare each transaction with a customer's history and with peer groups, then send the highest risk cases to human reviewers. Procurement teams use matching and anomaly detection to spot duplicate invoices, unusual vendor details, and payments that split just below approval limits. Investigators use graph methods to connect people, companies, accounts, and devices across datasets that would be too large to review by hand. Communication forensics applies language models and search to email, chat, and call records, often to reconstruct intent and sequence.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are mature. Rule engines and supervised models reliably catch known patterns, such as duplicate expense receipts, round number invoices, and payments to accounts that appear only once. Graph analysis has made money laundering networks easier to see, because it can link shared addresses, phone numbers, and beneficial owners across records. The unsolved parts are harder, since fraudsters change tactics, models drift, and false positives remain costly. Encrypted messaging, privacy coins, mixers, and cross border gaps limit what any system can see, and a flagged transaction is not proof of a crime. The wider atlas tracks 222 compliance and regulation pages, which reflects how much of this work depends on rules about data access, reporting, and evidence, and courts still require human testimony and a clear chain of custody.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages in this section divide the work by target and by method. Expense Fraud covers employee claims, corporate cards, and reimbursement schemes, so a reader goes there for the controls and models that catch small, repeated losses. Money Laundering Networks covers the larger graph problem, including layering, shell structures, and the network views that connect many accounts and entities. Phantom Vendors and Procurement Fraud covers fake suppliers, bid rigging, and invoice schemes, which is where vendor master data, purchase orders, and payment approvals meet. Communication Forensics covers email, chat, and metadata analysis, and it is the place to look for how language models and search help investigators reconstruct who knew what and when. Tracing and Recovering Digital Assets covers blockchain analysis, exchange records, and recovery efforts, so it serves readers who need to follow value after it leaves a bank account. Together these pages move from the smallest expense line to the widest network and then to the asset trail.
